transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for fitting me in. I, um... well, I'm a registered nurse, and honestly, things have just gotten so difficult at work lately that I felt like I had to come in before something bad happens. 

The main reason I’m here is that, when I'm on the floor, I just lose my train of thought constantly. And I mean constantly. It’s like my brain just completely resets without my permission. I’ll be right in the middle of something really important, like trying to figure out a complicated patient flow issue—you know, trying to juggle who is discharging, who needs transport, who is coming up from the ED—and then an IV pump starts beeping three rooms down. Or I'll just overhear someone asking another nurse a totally random question at the nurse's station, or a call light goes off, and... poof. It's just gone. 

Suddenly I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was even working on. I'll just be standing there with my computer open, totally blank, trying to retrace my mental steps while there's a million things happening around me. It's terrifying, honestly, because in my job you really can't afford to just forget what you're doing, but every little noise or interruption just completely derails me, and it takes me so much extra time just to figure out where I left off. It's exhausting.
Have you noticed any other changes in how your body feels or moves when these episodes happen—like trouble with coordination, dizziness, numbness, or weakness in any part of your body?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, as a nurse, my brain obviously goes straight to, you know, TIA or some kind of weird focal seizure or early-onset neurological thing when you ask that, but no. Physically, my body feels completely normal. I don't get dizzy, I don't have any tingling or numbness anywhere, no weakness in my arms or legs. 

My coordination is totally fine, too—like, mechanically, my hands know exactly what to do. I can still perfectly prime IV tubing or do a tricky blood draw without fumbling at all. It's not a physical clumsiness or a physical deficit in any way. It's literally just... the thought is gone. 

Which is almost more frustrating, honestly? Because if I were getting dizzy or weak, at least I could sit down and tell my charge nurse, "Hey, I'm having a medical moment, I need a break." But physically I'm standing right there, perfectly healthy, perfectly capable of moving, just staring blankly at a Pyxis machine because my brain just entirely deleted why I walked into the med room in the first place. I even did a quick little cranial nerve check on myself in the bathroom mirror a few weeks ago just because I was getting so paranoid about how often I was spacing out, but everything is totally intact. So, yeah, no physical changes at all. Just that complete mental blankness.
During these episodes where you lose your train of thought, do you ever feel like you're not fully aware of what's going on around you, or do you ever lose consciousness, even briefly?

No, definitely not. I've never lost consciousness or passed out or anything like that. And I don't think I lose awareness of what's going on around me, either. In fact, it almost feels like the exact opposite of that? It's like I'm too aware of everything around me. 

Like I was saying before, the whole reason I lose my train of thought is because I become hyper-aware of something else, like that IV pump down the hall, or a conversation at the desk, or even just someone walking past the door with a squeaky shoe. It's not that I'm zoning out into some kind of void where I don't know where I am or what's happening. It's that my attention just gets violently hijacked by whatever random stimulus just happened in my environment. 

So I'm fully awake, fully conscious, fully oriented to time and place and person, you know? I know I'm at work, I know who my patients are—well, mostly—and I know what I'm supposed to be doing, generally speaking. It's just that the specific task I was in the middle of gets completely erased because my brain decided that the squeaky shoe or the call light was suddenly the most urgent and important thing in the universe. 

I've never had a moment where I sort of "came to" and didn't know how much time had passed, or felt confused about where I was, or had anyone tell me I looked like I was having an absence seizure or staring off into space unresponsively. If someone says my name when I'm standing there trying to remember what I was doing, I snap right to them and answer immediately. So, yeah, no loss of consciousness, no blacking out, no missing time. Just... a really, really frustrating inability to hold onto a thought when literally anything else is happening around me.
Outside of these episodes at work, do you find yourself feeling anxious or worried most of the time, even when things aren't particularly stressful?

No, actually, no. I mean, I know I probably sound incredibly wound up right now talking about the hospital, but honestly... outside of work, or outside of situations where I have to juggle a bunch of important tasks, I don't feel anxious at all. I'm really not a worrier by nature. 

Like, I don't sit at home on my days off dreading the future or agonizing over random things. If I don't have anywhere to be and nothing specific I have to get done, I'm actually incredibly relaxed. My husband always jokes that I have exactly two modes—either I'm in full-blown crisis-management mode because I'm terrified of dropping the ball at work, or I'm practically a puddle on the couch. Like this past Sunday, we didn't have any errands to run, which is so rare, and I just sat out on the deck with a cup of coffee for literally three hours. I wasn't worrying about a single thing. I mean, sure, I probably didn't finish my coffee before it got cold because I kept getting distracted by the neighbor's dog or whatever, but I wasn't *stressed* about it. There was no dread, no tight chest, no racing thoughts about what-ifs. 

As a nurse, I see patients with generalized anxiety all the time, and they have that constant, humming sense of worry even when they're safe at home, and I definitely don't have that. My anxiety is completely tied to the fact that I feel like I can't trust my own brain when it actually matters. It's the fear of making a mistake on the floor because I lost my train of thought. But if there are no stakes? If it doesn't matter if I forget why I walked into the kitchen at home? I couldn't care less. I'm totally fine. So, yeah, I just wanted to make sure I made that distinction really clear, because I'm not just a nervous person in general. It's really just the frustration of my brain not cooperating when I need it to that makes me feel so overwhelmed.

Do you also experience difficulty holding onto your thoughts or getting distracted by small things in other parts of your life, like at home or during leisure activities, even if it doesn’t feel as critical or stressful as at work?

Oh, absolutely. It happens everywhere. Honestly, that's exactly what I meant when I was talking about the coffee on the deck—I get distracted by literally everything, no matter where I am. It just doesn't cause me the same level of panic when I'm at home because the stakes are so much lower, you know? But the actual mechanism of it? The losing my train of thought? That is a constant, 24/7 thing for me. 

Like, the main reason I’m here, the reason I finally made this appointment, is because of how bad it is on the floor—I mean, I lose my train of thought constantly at work. An IV pump beeps three rooms down, or someone asks another nurse a question at the charting station, or a call light goes off, and suddenly I’ve completely forgotten what patient flow issue I was working on. And that's terrifying because it's patient care. But the exact same thing happens at home, just with different triggers. 

I'll be in the middle of cooking dinner, and I'll walk into the pantry to get a can of diced tomatoes, and on the way, I'll notice that the dog's water bowl is empty. So I pick up the bowl, fill it, put it down, and then I'll see a piece of mail on the counter that I meant to open yesterday. I'll open the mail, realize it's a bill, go to my laptop to pay it, and then twenty minutes later I'll smell something burning and realize I left the onions on the stove and I never actually got the tomatoes. And I wasn't stressed during any of that! I was just... bouncing from one thing to the next because whatever caught my eye last completely erased whatever I was doing first. 

Or even during leisure activities, like you said. I try to read—I used to love reading—but I'll be reading a book, and my husband will flip a page in his magazine, or a car will drive by outside, and I'll realize I've "read" the same paragraph four times without actually absorbing a single word because my brain just followed the sound of the car down the street. So, yes, the distractibility is everywhere. It's just that at home, a burnt onion is the worst-case scenario, whereas at the hospital, forgetting why I walked into a room could actually hurt someone. But the inability to just hold onto a single thought without it getting knocked out of my head by something else? Yeah, that never turns off.
